name: Basilisk, Greater
desc: The feared greater basilisks are known by the tribesmen of the Sar'Lor Mountains as “stone dragons”, as unlike their lesser cousins, these terrifying lizards actually do have the power to turn a creature to stone. Anyone who falls under the gaze of a greater basilisk must make an opposed Willpower roll against the basilisk's Gaze skill to keep their eyes averted; failing results in transfor- mation into a living statue for up to several days. In stone form, the person is in a kind of unconscious stasis and does not feel the effects of hunger, sleep deprivation, environmental effects, or anything else. However, whatever damage is done to their statue form is reflected on the person upon recovery; this can often prove fatal. Luckily, the greater basilisks are reclusive creatures who mostly rely on fear of their petrifying gaze to keep predators away. A cadre of local tribal warriors known as the “Eyeless” have taken to training these creatures as mounts. But even they steer clear of the highest mountain peaks in the Sar'Lor range, for there are rumors of a terrifying “true” basilisk species lairing up there, whose petrifying effect lasts for years.

name: Brutesworn (Brakk-Thuun)
desc: The Brutesworn ( Brakk-Thuun in Tusker) are a de- generate offshoot of the Ogre species-descendants of ancient clans whose entire bloodlines collapsed into the Breaking and never recovered. Over gener- ations, that psychic catastrophe became hereditary, warping both mind and body. A Brutesworn resem- bles an Ogre only in silhouette: hunched, over- muscled, with a jutting bone-cracker jaw and long, dragging arms built for tearing prey apart. Their skin is thick and swollen and their tusks serrated, though they do not possess the swirling horns of the Ogres. They do not speak, laugh, or think in anything approaching reason. What remains is instinctive cunning, a predator's focus, and a compulsion to feed on anything living. They drift in loose mobs rather than true packs, drawn together by the scent of blood or the prom- ise of slaughter. When roused, a Brutesworn charge is less a coordinated attack than a devouring stampede-clumsy, loud, and utterly unstoppa- ble until every source of meat is consumed. Among Ogres, the Brutesworn are a glimpse of what their people might become if the Breaking ever fully triumphs.

name: Dark Fae: Queen's Huntsman
desc: When a Replaced escapes captivity and finds his or her way through the Thorns, the Dark Fae send forth the Queen's Hunt, a pack of four or five misshapen faerie creatures whose sole purpose is to track down the Replaced and bring them back to the Fae Queen. Though they take on many shapes, they are all gifted with the power of glamour and illusion so as to hide their true nature from the world at large. But if a Huntsman is ever viewed in a reflec- tive surface-a mirror, a placid pond, the eyes of an innocent-the creature's true form can be seen. For this reason, they avoid such reflective surfaces and will momentarily recoil from a mirror, giving a victim a brief opportunity to flee. This clever trick only effectively works the first time a Huntsman is encountered: each further use gives the Huntsman a +20 on the Willpower roll. Huntsmen will try to take their quarry alive, seeking to render them Unconscious or in Shock so they may transport them back beyond the Thorns. The Huntsman detailed below is but one typical humanoid example. They can look like small gob- lin-like creatures, wolves with heads of vultures, hulking hairy Ogre-like brutes, or anything else.

name: Ghost
desc: When someone of strong will is murdered, dies through another's negligence, or meets an unusual or mysterious end, there is a small chance their spirit resists the call to the next world and instead remains to haunt either the killer, or the place of their death. Ghosts are perpetually trapped within the moment of their demise, reliving the moment over and over again in their undead minds. They may freely project the pain and suffering of their torment onto the person (or anyone in the area) they are haunting. This pre- vents the victims from getting any sleep for as long as the ghost persists. Their wail of misery and anger can cause fear and physically age anyone it's directed at, causing necrotic wounds. The wail can be used once per victim, per encounter. Critically failing a resistance roll to the wail turns the victim's hair stark white. Not all ghosts are aggressive. Some even experience a form of supernatural dementia, with brief “mo- ments of clarity” where they suddenly understand that they are no longer alive, but not altogether dead either. These moments rarely last, but they present an opportunity: in its brief lucidity, the ghost could reveal a truth about its fate that could allow the living to help the tormented creature find release. “Killing” a ghost only causes it to reform between a day and a year later, depending on the ghost. A ghost cannot be permanently dispatched until the cause of its death is revealed and it believes justice has been done.

name: Half Giant (Fomor)
desc: The twisted, malformed giants known as the Fomor are the forgotten debased cousins of both the Bolg Fiir and the Duanan Seethe. The half giants stand almost 8 feet tall, with patches of coarse hair spottily covering their warty flesh. Hunchbacks, bulbous uneven eyes, and other deformities dominate their appearance, and they have a pungent odor that often heralds their ap- pearance. Half giants are filled with a hatred of most other living things (especially their fairer kin, the Bolg Fiir), and they have the unholy strength to tear a man in half. name: Highland Giant
desc: Before the race of Men came and imposed their will on the Weave, the giants were friends to the Dwarves, and almost as highly regarded for their architectural prowess. It was they who first taught the Dwarves how to build the magnificent stone arches and domes so often seen in ancient Dwarven craftsmanship. Alas, the magical raising of the Iron Veil took its toll upon the gentle giant folk, somehow rendering them into little more than simple-minded cave-dwellers. No one knows the causal connection between the world-shak- ing magics used to create the Veil and the fall of the giants, but today, all that is left of their artisanal heri- tage are overgrown ruins of towers and castles, hidden away in the secret places of the world. As they are now, the giants of the Broken Empires are 12-15' tall solitary creatures who keep to them- selves most of the time. Foolish is the adventurer who unknowingly sets foot in a giant's cave, for their fury at having their home invaded is terrifying to behold. Their hide is tough, granting them vari- able AP on their hit locations, as indicated. Loremasters claim that Highland giants have a peculiar vulnerability to the long-forgotten songs and stories of their ancient past. If a giant hears anyone singing the Dwarven songs of old Mountainholme, sung in the original Kharzhad, it must make a Willpower roll opposed to the singer's Perform . Failure indicates it sinks to the ground, morose and full of nostalgic despair, unwilling to fight any further unless its life continues to be threatened.

desc: A Husk is what remains of an Ironlander reaver who abandons his humanity in pursuit of a goal fueled by rage and vengeance. It is neither living, nor dead, nor undead. In fact, Loremasters are puzzled as to what fell force compels the Husk onwards to complete its foul purpose. Whatever that may be, a Husk is an implaca- ble foe that will drive itself to the ends of the earth in pursuit of its goal. Occasionally, desperate vikings and raiders of the very lowest character will fall into the service of a Husk as it relentlessly pursues its quarry. Once per combat, a Husk can emit a horrifying wail that causes fear in anyone within Medium range. A Husk also has the power to cause visions of paralyzing terror. This is a special action, opposed by Willpower , where every DoS Paralyzes the foe for 1 round. The victim may make a new resistance against the original roll every round to break free.

name: Lich
desc: A Spellweaver's greatest enemy is the Fraying, the inexplicable and inevitable fate that awaits all those who gain too much of the Weave's attention. Though many have tried to find a solution to the Fraying, all have failed-and none more spectacu- larly than those who wind up as a terrifying undead monster known as a lich (pronounced litch ). A lich is a powerful Spellweaver who, in seeking an escape from the Weave's final notice, has instead found an eternity of undeath, trapped in a prison of their own corpse. It is frightening, and its very touch radiates a damaging, supernatural cold that bypasses armor and causes “Cold” wounds. Its un- earthly power gives it 2 AP everywhere. A lich hides the remains of their mortal essence in a receptacle known as a phylactery: a magic-infused jar, box, or other container containing what remains of the lich's soul. A lich cannot be truly slain unless its phylactery is found and destroyed; otherwise, its body dissolves and reforms again next to its phylactery three nights after it is “killed”. Naturally, liches keep their phylacteries well-hidden and guarded. The secrets to making the transformation to li- chdom are known to very few, but those Spellweav- ers who are successful add the lich template, below.

name: Orc
desc: Their origins lost in the mists of time, the orcs of the Broken Empires are, with rare exception, savage raiders with an irrational hatred for all other races. There are no females or children among them; they are birthed fully grown from amniotic sacs in underground lairs. They emerge armed with an instinct for slaughter, carrying within them the fury of countless predecessors. They are not a people, but a contagion. Each warbrood-known in their own black tongue as a Vrul -is driven by the will of a distant Ulgath (“Bloodfather”), its unseen progenitor. Beneath him march the Skarns (“Underfangs”), the great enforc- ers who drive the lesser orcs to battle. They are biological war machines, bred for car- nage-but bred by whom? And for what purpose? Some say the orcs appeared alongside Humans when they first emerged from the south; others, that they were the product of a Duanan Seethe rit- ual gone wrong; still others suggest they are a kind of invasive species not of this world at all. Whatever their origin, the orcs are a blight upon all lands, a hatred made flesh that can never truly be destroyed.

name: Void Demon
desc: The Tapestry encompasses all of reality, but there are places outside the Tapestry, collectively known as the Void (also called Hell, Limbo, Oblivion, the Place Of Non-Being, and many other names). Creatures from the Void are known to Loremasters by many classifications, but the uneducated simply call them demons. These otherworldly beings have no form of their own and take shape only after crossing over into our world and invading a host body. When they do, they become ravenous for all the experiences available to a material form: flesh, wine, food, laugh- ter, rage, pain-they desire all of it, all at once, and in voracious quantities. A Void demon is a frenzy of insanely contradictory actions: one moment adoring- ly caressing an innocent, the next tearing the flesh from its skull in orgiastic laughter. Each demon has a True Name, which can be used to contact and summon it through Weave Magic, or, more rarely, through a direct pact with the demon itself. If summoned into a magic summon- ing circle, there must be a host body waiting to contain the entity. When a Void demon (intentionally summoned or not) forcibly inhabits a host-they prefer Humans, but will gladly invade the body of any available creature-it traps the being's mind in a prison of its own skull, slowly corrupting and distorting the flesh until it resembles a grotesque cross between the host's original form and some eldritch creature out of nightmare. To do this, the Void demon must win an opposed Willpower roll against the victim. The next round, the demon will possess the host and be- gin to manifest , which is a process lasting anywhere from a few weeks to a few moments. No two Void demons manifest in exactly the same way, but very often the host's eyes will go complete- ly black, and its skin will become hot to the touch until it inevitably bursts into black flame, sloughing off the bones. A pair of extra-long, taloned arms erupt from the host's midsection, and the being grows several feet taller. Spiny wings explode from its back, and the jaw becomes elongated and filled with row upon row of tearing teeth. Yet still the original host is identifiable within the ruined form, and the demon will always resemble it on some basic level. Hence, a Dwarf-demon is immediately distinctive from a Human-demon-although if they could, either would beg for death, the only release possible from the twisted prison the host's own body has become. It is difficult to save someone possessed by a de- mon. Attacking the body will only damage the host, and killing it will simply free the Void demon's essence to return from whence it came. To hurt the demon directly requires Spheres magic, to which a demon is vulnerable. The remains of a Void de- mon's host often act as a Spheres Thread. There is, according to Loremasters and knowledge- able Spellweavers, a breed of greater demon, which possesses a physical form outside the bounds of reality (a paradox necessary to the discussion of such things), and which can be physically summoned and commanded (or at least consulted). Such a summons would surely be performed under only the most desperate of situations… Below is a typical example of a fully transformed Human-demon.

name: Werewolf
desc: Lycanthropy is a parasitic disease that temporarily transforms a humanoid into a hulking, ferocious hu- manoid wolf-like creature. This metamorphosis oc- curs three nights after infection, and then again on random nights when any part of the moon is visible. The disease causes a frenzied need in the host crea- ture to infect others through its bite. Consequently, a werewolf will often attack from stealth and retreat as soon as it has bitten a new victim. When the sun rises, the host creature transforms back into its original humanoid form, retaining no memories of either the transformation or its nocturnal activities. Only silver weapons can permanently kill a trans- formed werewolf. When slain by silver, the parasite is forced from the host's body as a black, oily liquid, leaving the host dead. Unless immediately doused with quicksilver, the parasite remains infectious and propels itself by pseudopod into the nearest sentient creature's mouth to infect it ( Dodge vs 3 to oppose). Damage over a transformed werewolf's Death Threshold from any other attack merely forces it back into its unconscious humanoid form and resets the damage taken to zero. The parasite remains dormant within the living host, who will transform again on a random upcoming moonlit night.

The disease causes a frenzied need in the host crea- ture to infect others through its bite. Consequently, a werewolf will often attack from stealth and retreat as soon as it has bitten a new victim. When the sun rises, the host creature transforms back into its original humanoid form, retaining no memories of either the transformation or its nocturnal activities. Only silver weapons can permanently kill a trans- formed werewolf. When slain by silver, the parasite is forced from the host's body as a black, oily liquid, leaving the host dead. Unless immediately doused with quicksilver, the parasite remains infectious and propels itself by pseudopod into the nearest sentient creature's mouth to infect it ( Dodge vs 3 to oppose). Damage over a transformed werewolf's Death Threshold from any other attack merely forces it back into its unconscious humanoid form and resets the damage taken to zero. The parasite remains dormant within the living host, who will transform again on a random upcoming moonlit night.
